subtopics.title: 1. Cell Biology
subtopics.method: Cells are the foundation of Biology. This topic links structure to function and explains how substances move, cells divide and microorganisms are studied.

sections.heading: Key definitions
list: Eukaryotic cell — a cell containing genetic material enclosed in a nucleus.
Prokaryotic cell — a smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
Differentiation — the process by which a cell changes to become specialised.
Diffusion — net movement of particles from high to low concentration.
Osmosis — net movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution.
Active transport — movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.

sections.heading: What you must know
list: Know organelles in animal, plant and bacterial cells and link each to function.
Compare light and electron microscopes; calculate magnification using image size ÷ real size.
Explain specialised cells such as sperm, nerve, muscle, root hair and xylem cells.
Describe the cell cycle, mitosis and why mitosis is important for growth and repair.
Understand stem cells, their potential uses and ethical considerations.
Explain factors affecting diffusion and compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

sections.heading: Process to explain — Mitosis
sections.text: DNA replicates → chromosomes are separated → nucleus divides → cytoplasm and cell membrane divide → two genetically identical daughter cells are produced.

sections.heading: Required practical
sections.text: Microscopy: prepare a slide, use stains where appropriate, focus from low to high power, calculate magnification. Osmosis: change solution concentration, measure mass/length before and after, calculate percentage change, control time/temperature/specimen size.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Confusing cell membrane with cell wall.
Saying osmosis is movement of 'particles' instead of water.
Forgetting that active transport requires energy.
Using magnification units inconsistently.

sections.heading: Exam-style question
sections.text: Explain how a root hair cell is adapted for the uptake of water and mineral ions.

sections.heading: Answer route
sections.text: Long extension gives large surface area; thin surface shortens diffusion distance; water enters by osmosis; mineral ions can be absorbed by active transport against their concentration gradient; many mitochondria provide energy for active transport.

subtopics.title: 2. Organisation
subtopics.method: Multicellular organisms contain specialised cells organised into tissues, organs and organ systems. This topic focuses heavily on digestion, circulation and plant transport.

sections.heading: Key definitions
list: Tissue — a group of similar cells working together to perform a function.
Organ — a group of different tissues working together.
Enzyme — a biological catalyst that speeds up reactions without being used up.
Denaturation — a permanent change in an enzyme's active site shape.
Transpiration — loss of water vapour from leaves, mainly through stomata.
Translocation — movement of dissolved sugars through phloem.

sections.heading: What you must know
list: Explain enzyme action using active site and specificity.
Know roles of amylase, protease and lipase and where they act.
Know the heart chambers, major blood vessels and double circulatory system.
Compare arteries, veins and capillaries.
Know blood components and their functions.
Understand coronary heart disease and treatments.
Know plant tissues: epidermal, palisade, spongy mesophyll, xylem, phloem and meristem.
Explain factors affecting transpiration.

sections.heading: Process to explain — Enzyme action
sections.text: Substrate with complementary shape binds to active site → enzyme-substrate complex forms → reaction occurs → products leave → enzyme can be reused. High temperature/extreme pH can alter the active site.

sections.heading: Required practical
sections.text: Food tests: iodine for starch, Benedict's + heat for reducing sugars, Biuret for protein, emulsion test for lipids. Enzymes: investigate the effect of pH on amylase using iodine and controlled temperature.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Saying enzymes are 'killed' rather than denatured.
Mixing up arteries and veins by oxygen content rather than direction of blood flow.
Forgetting capillaries have thin walls for exchange.
Confusing xylem with phloem.

sections.heading: Exam-style question
sections.text: Explain how the structure of a capillary is adapted for exchange with body tissues.

sections.heading: Answer route
sections.text: Wall is one cell thick → short diffusion distance; narrow lumen keeps blood cells close to the wall; extensive capillary networks give large surface area; slow blood flow allows time for exchange; concentration gradients allow diffusion.

subtopics.title: 3. Infection and Response
subtopics.method: This topic explains how pathogens cause disease, how the body defends itself and how medicines and vaccination reduce disease.

sections.heading: Key definitions
list: Pathogen — a microorganism that causes infectious disease.
Communicable disease — a disease that can spread between organisms.
Antigen — a molecule on a pathogen that triggers an immune response.
Antibody — a protein produced by lymphocytes that binds specifically to an antigen.
Vaccination — introducing harmless pathogen material/antigens to stimulate immunity.
Antibiotic — a medicine that kills bacteria or stops their growth.

sections.heading: What you must know
list: Compare viral, bacterial, fungal and protist diseases.
Know examples such as measles, HIV, TMV, salmonella, gonorrhoea, malaria and rose black spot.
Explain non-specific defences: skin, mucus/cilia, stomach acid.
Explain phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxins.
Explain vaccination and herd effects at GCSE level.
Understand antibiotics, resistance and why antibiotics do not treat viruses.
Know stages of drug development: discovery, preclinical testing, clinical trials, dose and efficacy.

sections.heading: Process to explain — Vaccination
sections.text: Pathogen antigens enter the body safely → lymphocytes produce specific antibodies → memory cells remain → on later infection, antibodies are produced rapidly → pathogen is destroyed before serious illness develops.

sections.heading: Required practical
sections.text: Culturing microorganisms: use sterile technique, sterilised agar and equipment, secure the lid appropriately, incubate school cultures at a safe temperature, measure zones of inhibition and compare antimicrobial effectiveness.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Saying antibiotics kill viruses.
Claiming vaccines guarantee nobody becomes infected.
Confusing antibodies with antigens.
Forgetting placebo/double-blind ideas in clinical trials.

sections.heading: Exam-style question
sections.text: Explain why overuse of antibiotics can increase the number of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

sections.heading: Answer route
sections.text: Random mutations create resistant variants; antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria; resistant bacteria survive; they reproduce and pass resistance genes on; resistant strain becomes more common — natural selection.

subtopics.title: 4. Bioenergetics
subtopics.method: Bioenergetics covers how organisms transfer energy through photosynthesis and respiration.

sections.heading: Key definitions
list: Photosynthesis — an endothermic reaction in which light energy is used to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Limiting factor — a factor in shortest supply that restricts the rate of a process.
Aerobic respiration — respiration using oxygen to release energy from glucose.
Anaerobic respiration — respiration without oxygen; releases less energy.
Oxygen debt — extra oxygen required after exercise to react with accumulated lactic acid.

sections.heading: What you must know
list: Know word and symbol equations for photosynthesis and aerobic respiration.
Explain effects of light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature on photosynthesis.
Know uses of glucose: respiration, cellulose, amino acids, starch and lipids.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in animals, plants and yeast.
Explain body responses to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase.
Explain metabolism as the sum of chemical reactions in cells.

sections.heading: Process to explain — Photosynthesis rate
sections.text: Increasing a limiting factor increases the rate until another factor becomes limiting. Temperature rises increase enzyme-controlled reactions up to an optimum; above this, enzymes denature and the rate falls.

sections.heading: Required practical
sections.text: Photosynthesis: use pondweed or another suitable plant, vary light intensity/distance, measure oxygen production over a fixed time, control temperature/CO₂/specimen, repeat and calculate a mean.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Writing that plants only respire at night.
Forgetting photosynthesis is endothermic.
Saying anaerobic respiration releases more energy.
Assuming a graph plateaus because the tested factor has 'stopped working' rather than another factor becoming limiting.

sections.heading: Exam-style question
sections.text: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis may stop increasing when light intensity continues to increase.

sections.heading: Answer route
sections.text: Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature limits the rate; photosynthetic enzymes/substrates cannot support a faster rate.

subtopics.title: 5. Homeostasis and Response
subtopics.method: Organisms detect changes and coordinate responses. This topic links the nervous system, hormones and control of internal conditions.

sections.heading: Key definitions
list: Homeostasis — regulation of internal conditions to maintain optimum conditions for cell function.
Receptor — a cell or organ that detects a stimulus.
Effector — a muscle or gland that produces a response.
Reflex — a rapid automatic response to a stimulus.
Hormone — a chemical messenger carried in the blood to a target organ.
Negative feedback — a control mechanism that reverses a change and returns a condition towards its normal level.

sections.heading: What you must know
list: Know the pathway: stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.
Explain reflex arcs and synapses.
Know brain regions at GCSE level and challenges of investigating brain function.
Explain eye accommodation and common vision defects where required.
Compare nervous and hormonal communication.
Explain blood glucose control by insulin and glucagon.
Know diabetes types and treatments.
Explain menstrual cycle hormones and fertility treatments/contraception.
Explain thermoregulation and water balance where required.

sections.heading: Process to explain — Blood glucose
sections.text: High glucose → pancreas releases insulin → cells take up glucose and liver/muscle convert glucose to glycogen → level falls. Low glucose → glucagon → glycogen converted to glucose → level rises.

sections.heading: Required practical
sections.text: Reaction time: measure response to a stimulus, repeat and calculate a mean, change one factor such as distraction/caffeine only if safe/appropriate, control participant/method/environment.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Mixing up receptor and effector.
Saying hormones travel through nerves.
Confusing insulin with glucagon.
Describing negative feedback as simply 'a negative response'.

sections.heading: Exam-style question
sections.text: Compare nervous communication with hormonal communication.

sections.heading: Answer route
sections.text: Nervous: electrical impulses along neurones, very fast, short-lived, precise target. Hormonal: chemicals carried in blood, slower, longer-lasting, can affect multiple target tissues with receptors.

subtopics.title: 6. Inheritance, Variation and Evolution
subtopics.method: This topic explains how genetic information is inherited, why organisms vary and how populations change over time.

sections.heading: Key definitions
list: Gene — a section of DNA that codes for a protein/characteristic.
Allele — a different version of a gene.
Genome — the entire genetic material of an organism.
Genotype — the alleles an organism possesses.
Phenotype — observable characteristics produced by genotype and environment.
Natural selection — process in which better-adapted organisms survive and reproduce more successfully.

sections.heading: What you must know
list: Know DNA, chromosomes, genes and genome relationships.
Use genetic crosses and probability for inherited characteristics.
Explain dominant/recessive alleles and homozygous/heterozygous genotypes.
Distinguish inherited and environmental variation.
Explain evolution by natural selection.
Understand selective breeding and genetic engineering.
Know evidence for evolution including fossils and resistant bacteria.
Understand classification and evolutionary relationships.

sections.heading: Process to explain — Natural selection
sections.text: Mutation creates variation → environmental selection pressure → individuals with advantageous phenotype survive more → reproduce → pass advantageous alleles to offspring → allele frequency increases over generations.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Saying organisms 'choose' to adapt.
Confusing genotype and phenotype.
Using dominant to mean 'more common' or 'stronger'.
Forgetting mutations are random.

sections.heading: Exam-style question
sections.text: Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic.

sections.heading: Answer route
sections.text: Random mutation gives resistance; antibiotic is the selection pressure; non-resistant bacteria die; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; resistance allele is passed on; proportion resistant increases over generations.

subtopics.title: 7. Ecology
subtopics.method: Ecology examines interactions between organisms and their environment, material cycles and the impact of humans on biodiversity.

sections.heading: Key definitions
list: Community — all populations of different species living and interacting in an ecosystem.
Ecosystem — interaction of a community of organisms with the non-living parts of their environment.
Biodiversity — variety of living organisms in an ecosystem or on Earth.
Producer — an organism that makes biomass, usually by photosynthesis.
Decomposer — a microorganism that breaks down dead material and waste.
Trophic level — a feeding level in a food chain or food web.

sections.heading: What you must know
list: Know biotic and abiotic factors affecting communities.
Explain adaptations and competition.
Use quadrats and transects to estimate distribution/abundance.
Interpret food chains, food webs and trophic levels.
Explain carbon and water cycles.
Explain decomposition and factors affecting it.
Understand biodiversity, land use, deforestation, global warming and conservation.
Understand biomass transfer and food security where required.

sections.heading: Process to explain — Carbon cycle
sections.text: CO₂ removed by photosynthesis → carbon passes through food chains → respiration returns CO₂ → death/waste are decomposed → decomposers respire → combustion of fuels/biomass releases CO₂.

sections.heading: Required practical
sections.text: Ecology fieldwork: random quadrat sampling for abundance; transects for changes across a gradient; identify variables, use enough samples, calculate means and describe limitations.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Calling a habitat an ecosystem without including interactions.
Assuming correlation proves causation in field data.
Forgetting random sampling reduces bias.
Confusing biomass with number of organisms.

sections.heading: Exam-style question
sections.text: Describe how you could estimate the population size of daisies in a large field.

sections.heading: Answer route
sections.text: Use a quadrat of known area; place quadrats randomly using coordinates; count daisies in many quadrats; calculate the mean number per quadrat; scale up using field area ÷ quadrat area; use many repeats for reliability and avoid biased placement.

subtopics.title: How to revise Biology for marks
subtopics.method: Learn the science, understand the process, then practise applying it. Read a section, cover it and recall aloud, then attempt an exam question before checking the answer route.

sections.heading: Five habits that earn marks
list: Learn precise definitions — mark schemes reward exact scientific vocabulary; do not replace key terms with vague everyday language.
Explain in chains — for 'explain' questions, build cause → mechanism → effect. One isolated fact rarely earns all the marks.
Know the practical logic — not just the method: the variables, why each control matters, how results are processed and how validity can be improved.
Use data — quote values, compare numbers and describe trends accurately. 'It goes up' is weaker than a quantified comparison.
Apply familiar science to unfamiliar contexts — the organism or scenario may look new, but diffusion, enzymes, inheritance, homeostasis and ecosystems are the same.

sections.heading: Last-minute rule
sections.text: Do not spend your final revision hours rereading. Recall from memory, answer questions, mark them, then target the gaps you actually find.

subtopics.title: Biology calculations you should know
formulae: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values
Surface area : volume — calculate surface area and volume separately, then simplify the ratio
Population estimate = mean organisms per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area)
subtopics.method: These are the calculations that recur across GCSE Biology. Learn each and practise on data from questions.

sections.heading: Unit warning
sections.text: Convert units before calculating. Common microscopy conversions: 1 mm = 1000 micrometres; 1 micrometre = 1000 nanometres.

subtopics.title: Required practicals — master summary
subtopics.method: The exact list depends on specification, but these are the high-value practical skills you should be able to describe, analyse and evaluate.

sections.heading: What to remember
list: Microscopy — prepare specimen/slide; focus low to high power; biological drawing; magnification = image size ÷ real size.
Osmosis — measure initial and final mass/length across concentrations; calculate percentage change; identify the isotonic point from a graph.
Food tests — know reagents, positive results, controls and safe heating for Benedict's test.
Enzymes — vary pH or temperature; control other variables; measure reaction time/rate; use repeats.
Photosynthesis — vary light intensity; measure oxygen production; control temperature, CO₂ and plant material.
Microbiology — aseptic technique; agar plates; antimicrobial discs; zones of inhibition; safe incubation.
Reaction time — standardised stimulus/response method; repeats and mean; control confounding variables.
Ecology — random quadrats, transects, abundance/distribution, representative sampling.

subtopics.title: Final GCSE Biology checklist
subtopics.method: Use this to confirm you can do each of these unaided before the exam.

sections.heading: I can…
list: Label and compare animal, plant and bacterial cells.
Explain diffusion, osmosis and active transport precisely.
Explain enzyme action and factors affecting enzymes.
Explain circulation and exchange surfaces.
Explain immune responses, vaccination and antibiotic resistance.
Write and interpret photosynthesis and respiration equations.
Explain homeostasis using negative feedback.
Complete genetic crosses and explain natural selection.
Explain food webs, cycles, biodiversity and sampling.
Describe required practicals with variables, controls, repeats and processing.
Interpret graphs and quote data accurately.
Answer 'explain' questions in linked cause → effect chains.
